claim: Low-intensity ultrasound at 5 mW/cm² (ISPTA) for 1 minute was able to activate neurons in the mouse brain, as evidenced by increased p-ERK positive cells in the cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala compared to sham treatment.
source: Mice with 1 min ultrasound exposure (Figure 1A) had shown significant increase of p-ERK positive cells in certain brain regions, such as the cortex (Figure 1B–D), hippocampus (Figure 1E–G), and amygdala (Figure 1H–J) as compared with those received sham treatment (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing p-ERK staining in brain sections and quantification showing significant differences (P = 0.0007 for cortex, P = 0.0132 for hippocampus, P = 0.0023 for amygdala).

claim: The ultrasound exposure was kept below 10 mW/cm² (ISATA) to ensure safe therapeutic applicability.
source: We kept ultrasound exposure to below 10 mW/cm2 (ISATA) in our experiments to ensure safe therapeutic applicability.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental design based on safety considerations.

claim: Increased p-ERK expression occurred in specific cortical areas including visual, somatosensory, auditory, temporal associations, retrosplenial, piriform, and entorhinal areas upon ultrasound stimulation.
source: More specifically, increased p-ERK expression generally occurred upon ultrasound stimulation in the visual, somatosensory, auditory, temporal associations, retrosplenial, piriform, and entorhinal areas of mouse cortex (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in supplementary figures showing regional p-ERK expression patterns.

claim: In hippocampus, CA1 and CA2 showed dramatic p-ERK signals in response to ultrasound whereas CA3 and dentate gyrus showed sparse stimulation.
source: In hippocampus, CA1 and CA2 were dramatically lightened up with p-ERK signals in response to ultrasound whereas CA3 and dentate gyrus showed sparsely stimulated (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from supplementary figures showing differential p-ERK responses in hippocampal subregions.

claim: The central amygdala nucleus showed the strongest p-ERK signals, while medial and basolateral amygdala also showed obvious increases in p-ERK signals.
source: In amygdala, the central amygdala nucleus showed the strongest p-ERK signals, while medial and basolateral also obviously increased in p-ERK signals (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from supplementary figures showing differential p-ERK responses in amygdala subregions.

claim: The paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus (PVH) showed consistently unchanged p-ERK staining, revealing regional specificity of the ultrasound response.
source: We also observed a consistently unchanged p-ERK staining in the paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus (PVH) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), revealing an intriguing regional specificity of the ultrasound response.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a supplementary figure showing no change in p-ERK in PVH, which is interpreted as evidence of regional specificity.

claim: A mixed loading condition (700 mVpp, 20% duty factor) combining ultrasound-induced pressure and acoustic streaming effectively yielded much higher calcium responses in cultured cortical neurons compared to pressure-predominant or streaming-predominant conditions alone.
source: Ultrasound pressure predominant conditions (up to 2000 mVpp, DF 0.05%) generated compressional stress on cells that were not able to elevate calcium responses (Figure 2B and Video 1), while acoustic streaming predominant conditions (up to 100 mVpp, DF 100%) invoked shear stress that could only activate little calcium responses in neurons (Figure 2B); whereas a mixed loading condition (700 mVpp, 20 % DF) effectively yielded much higher calcium responses (Figure 2B and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing calcium imaging results under different ultrasound conditions.

claim: The ultrasound-induced calcium responses were dose-dependent with a threshold of 400 mVpp (8 kPa) and EC50 of 700 mVpp (12 kPa).
source: The ultrasound-induced calcium responses were dose-dependent with a threshold of 400 mVpp (8 kPa) and EC50 of 700 mVpp (12 kPa) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 4D-K).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in figures.

claim: Gadolinium (120 μM), a non-selective blocker of mechanically sensitive ion channels, partially suppressed ultrasound-induced calcium signals in cortical neurons.
source: First, the treatment with Gadolinium (10 μM), a non-selective blocker of mechanically sensitive ion channels, partially suppressed the ultrasound-induced calcium signals (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of gadolinium treatment on calcium responses.

claim: GsMTx-4 (500 nM), a selective Piezo inhibitor, led to a marginal (not significant) inhibition of ultrasound-induced calcium elevation.
source: Treating the cells with a selective Piezo inhibitor, GsMTx-4, led to a marginal (not significant) inhibition of the ultrasound-induced calcium elevation as compared with the vehicle control (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing minimal effect of GsMTx-4 on calcium responses.

claim: Ruthenium red (1–10 μM), a TRP blocker, partially suppressed ultrasound-induced calcium signals.
source: Instead, the treatment with a TRP blocker ruthenium red (1–10 μM) partially suppressed the calcium signals (Figure 2F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of ruthenium red treatment on calcium responses.

claim: Amiloride, a non-selective ASIC inhibitor, totally abolished the calcium signals induced by micropipette ultrasound.
source: whereas the non-selective ASIC inhibitor, amiloride, totally abolished the calcium signals by micropipette ultrasound (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing complete inhibition of calcium responses by amiloride.

claim: PcTx1 (50 nM), an ASIC1a inhibitor, significantly inhibited the calcium response induced by micropipette ultrasound.
source: PcTx1 (50 nM) significantly inhibited the calcium response by micropipette ultrasound (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of PcTx1 treatment on calcium responses.

claim: The IC50 of PcTx1 for inhibiting micropipette ultrasound-induced responses was 0.2 nM, suggesting a homotrimeric ASIC1a is the mechanoreceptor in action.
source: We further tested the dose-dependent inhibition of PcTx1 on micropipette ultrasound and determined an IC50 of 0.2 nM, suggesting a homotrimeric ASIC1a is the mechanoreceptor in action (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 A-F).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data and inference based on known PcTx1 sensitivity of ASIC1a homotrimers.

claim: Extracellular calcium influx was absolutely essential for ultrasound-induced calcium responses, as shown by treatment with EGTA (1–5 mM).
source: To validate how ASIC1a activation would lead to calcium responses to ultrasound, we treated the cells with calcium chelating agent, ethylene glycol-bis(β-aminoethyl ether)-N,N,N′,N′-tetraacetic acid (EGTA) (1–5 mM) to block the extracellular calcium. The results showed that calcium influx was absolutely essential (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing complete inhibition of calcium responses by EGTA.

claim: The RyR inhibitor JTV519 fumarate (10 μM) partially inhibited the calcium surge, while the IP3R inhibitor (-)-Xestonspongin C (1 μM) was most inhibitory.
source: To examine whether endoplasmic reticulum calcium was involved in calcium signaling, we found the calcium surge of cells treated with the RyR inhibitor, JTV519 fumarate (10 μM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and I) was partially inhibited, while as the IP3R inhibitor, (-)-Xestonspongin C (1 μM) was most inhibited (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of RyR and IP3R inhibitors on calcium responses.

claim: Cytochalasin D (5–10 μg/ml), an actin polymerization inhibitor, dose-dependently and significantly suppressed the calcium response stimulated by micropipette ultrasound.
source: We likewise treated the cells with either actin polymerization inhibitor, cytochalasin D (5–10 μg/ml) or microtubule assembly inhibitor, nocodazole (5–10 μg/ml). Indeed, inhibition of cytoskeletal dynamics could dose dependently and significantly suppress the calcium response stimulated by micropipette ultrasound (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent inhibition by cytochalasin D.

claim: Nocodazole (5–10 μg/ml), a microtubule assembly inhibitor, dose-dependently and significantly suppressed the calcium response stimulated by micropipette ultrasound.
source: We likewise treated the cells with either actin polymerization inhibitor, cytochalasin D (5–10 μg/ml) or microtubule assembly inhibitor, nocodazole (5–10 μg/ml). Indeed, inhibition of cytoskeletal dynamics could dose dependently and significantly suppress the calcium response stimulated by micropipette ultrasound (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent inhibition by nocodazole.

claim: CHO cells transfected with Asic1 cDNA showed an immediate calcium response to micropipette-guided ultrasound, while mock-transfected cells showed a delayed calcium response.
source: Interestingly, CHO cells might contain some endogenous mechanosensitive machinery that can manifest a delayed calcium response to micropipette-guided ultrasound (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). In contrast, Asic1-transfected cells showed an immediate calcium response to the ultrasound (Figure 4A–C, Video 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating a role for ASIC1a in the ultrasound-mediated mechanotransduction (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing calcium responses in Asic1-transfected versus mock-transfected CHO cells.

claim: Two-way ANOVA analysis showed both ASIC1a overexpression and ultrasound treatments significantly regulated the calcium response of CHO cells.
source: Two-way ANOVA analysis showed both ASIC1a overexpression and ultrasound treatments significantly regulated the calcium response of CHO cells (Supplementary file 1) and the p value was 0.086 for the interaction of the two factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: PcTx1 treatment did not affect the ultrasound-induced delayed calcium responses in vehicle transfected CHO cells.
source: Note that PcTx1 treatment did not affect the ultrasound-induced delayed calcium responses in vehicle transfected cells (Figure 4E), as ultrasound as a factor still contributed significantly (F = 17.2; p < 0.0001) to the changes of calcium while there was no significant (F = 1.44; p = 0.15) (Supplementary file 1) interaction of drug treatments with ultrasound stimulations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis showing no effect of PcTx1 on vehicle-transfected cells.

claim: PcTx1 significantly inhibited ultrasound-induced calcium responses in Asic1-transfected CHO cells.
source: In contrast, PcTx1 significantly inhibited ultrasound-induced calcium responses in Asic1-transfected cells (Figure 4F) (F = 1.26; p = 0.29) (Supplementary file 1), while the two factors interact significantly (F = 4.46, p < 0.0001) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis showing significant inhibition by PcTx1 in Asic1-transfected cells.

claim: After three consecutive days of 5 min ultrasound treatments (5 mW/cm²), DCX staining in dentate gyrus at day 4 and day 7 showed a significant twofold increase compared to non-treated controls.
source: Compared to the non-treated controls, after three consecutive days of 5 min ultrasound treatments (5 mW/cm2), DCX staining in dentate gyrus at day 4 and day seven showed a significant twofold increase (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased DCX-positive cells in dentate gyrus after ultrasound treatment.

claim: Repeated stimulation of low-intensity ultrasound on mouse brain might achieve beneficial neural modulation and lead to neurogenesis in dentate gyrus.
source: The results indicated that repeated stimulation of low-intensity ultrasound on mouse brain might achieve beneficial neural modulation and lead to neurogenesis in dentate gyrus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCX staining results, based on the established role of DCX as a neurogenesis marker.

claim: The increase of DCX staining upon ultrasound stimulation was partially compromised in Asic1-/- mice.
source: We observed a reproducibly significant increase of DCX staining in the ultrasound treated group while quantification and student t-test analysis indicated that the increase was partially compromised in Asic1-/- (Figure 6A–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing DCX staining in wildtype versus Asic1-/- mice after ultrasound treatment.

claim: Two-way ANOVA analysis showed that ultrasound treatment (F = 9.4; p = 0.0098) and Asic1-/- (F = 26.35; p = 0.0002) significantly regulated DCX-positive cell counts, with no significant interaction (F = 0.22; p = 0.65) between these two factors.
source: We tested whether there was an interaction between the two factors, that is the two-way ANOVA analysis results showed that the ultrasound treatment (F = 9.4; p = 0.0098) and the Asic1-/- (F = 26.35; p = 0.0002) in regulating the DCX-positive cell counts (Supplementary file 1). In addition, there was no significant interaction (F = 0.22; p = 0.65) of these two factors while both factors contributed significantly and independently to the DCX cell counts (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The p-ERK cell count increase in Asic1-/- mice was partially decreased in hippocampal region while greatly reduced in cortical and amygdala regions compared to wildtype mice upon transcranial ultrasound stimulation.
source: Comparing to the mock controls (Figure 7C, J and Q), the cell counts increase of p-ERK staining in Asic1-/- was partially decreased in hippocampal region while greatly reduced in cortical and amygdala regions (Figure 7D, K and R).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing p-ERK responses in wildtype versus Asic1-/- mice.

claim: The reduction of p-ERK cell counts caused the difference between mock control and ultrasound stimulation to be statistically insignificant in Asic1-/- mice.
source: The reduction of p-ERK cell counts caused the difference between mock control and ultrasound stimulation to be statistically insignificant in Asic1-/- mice (Figure 7G, N and U).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data showing no significant difference in Asic1-/- mice.

claim: Asic3-/- mice showed a more consistent lower background of p-ERK in mock controls and exhibited a significant increase of p-ERK cell counts in response to ultrasound treatment.
source: On the other hand, Asic3-/- mice showed a more consistent lower background of p-ERK in mock controls (Figure 7E, L and S) and exhibited a significant increase of p-ERK cell counts (Figure 7F, M and T) to the ultrasound treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing p-ERK responses in Asic3-/- mice.

claim: Two-way ANOVA analysis showed an interaction of genotype and ultrasound treatment in the cortex (F = 6.45, p = 0.0037) but not in hippocampus and amygdala.
source: The two-way ANOVA analysis of p-ERK cell counts showed that there was only an interaction of two factors, namely genotype and ultrasound treatment in the cortex (F = 6.45, p = 0.0037) but not in hippocampus and amygdala (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The p-ERK response in mouse brain is likely directly caused by transcranial ultrasound instead of secondary effects due to neurons wired with auditory or other sensory circuits, as ASIC3 is mainly expressed in somatosensory neurons and spiral ganglion neurons.
source: These results indicated that the p-ERK response in mouse brain is likely directly caused by the transcranial ultrasound instead of caused by the secondary effects due to the neurons wired with auditory circuits or other sensory circuits, as ASIC3 being mainly expressed in somatosensory neurons and spiral ganglion neurons (Lin et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the Asic3-/- data combined with knowledge about ASIC3 expression patterns from cited literature.

claim: 94% (197/209) of p-ERK positive cells co-stained with NeuN.
source: NeuN+ in p-ERK population was 94% (197/209)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence co-staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4.5% (10/223) of p-ERK positive cells co-stained with GAD67.
source: GAD67+ in p-ERK population was 4.5% (10/223)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence co-staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: 0.9% (2/211) of p-ERK positive cells co-stained with PV.
source: PV+ in p-ERK population was 0.9% (2/211)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence co-staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: ASICs are involved in different types of mechanotransduction in the sensory nervous system, including nociception, baroreception, proprioception, and hearing.
source: Accumulating evidence has shown ASICs are involved in different types of mechanotransduction in the sensory nervous system, including nociception, baroreception, proprioception, and hearing (Cheng et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2016; Chen and Wong, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ASIC1a is a predominant acid sensor modulating neural activity in physiological and pathological conditions.
source: although ASIC1a is a predominant acid sensor modulating neural activity in physiological and pathological conditions (Baron and Lingueglia, 2015; Wemmie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Low-intensity ultrasound could modulate neural activity in mouse brain and directly activate neurons via an ASIC1a-dependent manner.
source: Here, we demonstrated low-intensity ultrasound could modulate neural activity in mouse brain and directly activate neurons (Figure 1) via an ASIC1a-depenent manner (Figures 2–3).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The current view of transcranial ultrasound activation of neurons in brain is through the auditory nerves.
source: While the current view of transcranial ultrasound activation of neurons in brain is through the auditory nerves (Sato et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Results from Asic3-/- mice suggest that peripheral nerves may not play a role in the activation of p-ERK in mouse brain by low intensity ultrasound.
source: our results from Asic3-/- mice suggest that the peripheral nerves may not play a role in the activation of p-ERK in mouse brain by low intensity ultrasound.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Asic3-/- experimental results.

claim: The low-intensity ultrasound-mediated mechanotransduction may act via a channel subtype-dependent manner specific for ASIC1a but not for other ASIC subtypes.
source: Alternatively, the low-intensity ultrasound-mediated mechanotransduction may act via a channel subtype-dependent manner specific for ASIC1a but not for other ASIC subtypes as shown in dextrose prolotherapy (Han et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by inference from the data and citation to related work.

claim: Repeated transcranial low-intensity ultrasound stimulations are safe and able to elicit adult neurogenesis in mouse brains.
source: Moreover, repeated transcranial low-intensity ultrasound stimulations are safe and able to elicit adult neurogenesis in mouse brains (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the DCX staining results and the use of low-intensity parameters.

claim: ASIC1a can form homotrimeric and heterotrimeric channels with different sensitivity to PcTx1 inhibition.
source: ASIC1a is widely expressed in the brain and could form as homotrimeric and heterotrimeric channels with different sensitivity to PcTx1 inhibition (Joeres et al., 2016; Sherwood et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Heterotrimeric ASIC2b/ASIC1a can be inhibited 50% by approximately 3 nM PcTx1.
source: Specifically, heterotrimeric ASIC2b/ASIC1a can be inhibited 50 % by approximately 3 nM (Sherwood et al., 2011) PcTx1
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ASIC1a/ASIC2a heterotrimeric channels can be inhibited by 50 nM PcTx1.
source: and ASIC1a/ASIC2a heterotrimeric can be inhibited by 50 nM (Joeres et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 0.5 nM to 1 nM PcTx1 can inhibit homotrimeric ASIC1a.
source: whereas 0.5 nM to 1 nM can inhibit the homotrimeric ASIC1a (Escoubas et al., 2003; Saez et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Since PcTx1 in low-doses effectively inhibited ASIC1a-mediated calcium signal by micropipette ultrasound, homotrimeric ASIC1a channels may be the predominant subtype involved in ultrasound mechanotransduction in cortical neurons.
source: Therefore, since PcTx1 in low-doses effectively inhibited ASIC1a-mediated calcium signal by micropipette ultrasound, homotrimeric ASIC1a channels may be the predominant subtype involved in ultrasound mechanotransduction in cortical neurons (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the IC50 data combined with knowledge about PcTx1 sensitivity of different ASIC1a channel configurations.

claim: In a mixed loading condition, the extracellular domains of ASIC1a are under shear force pulling the protein to the flow direction while the intracellular domains are connected to cortical actin or other cytoskeleton, which experiences dynamic reorganization coupling with membrane withdrawals in response to ultrasound.
source: Considering the combinatorial forces mode in vitro, we argue, in a mixed loading condition (Figures 2B and 3 F), the extracellular domains of ASIC1a are under shear force pulling the protein to the flow direction while the intracellular domains of the ASIC1a are connected to cortical actin or other cytoskeleton, which experiences dynamic reorganization coupling with membrane withdrawals in response to ultrasound (Chu et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the experimental data and citations to related work on cytoskeletal dynamics.

claim: Mechano-signal triggered ASIC1a, essentially a sodium channel, results in intracellular calcium elevation possibly by activating voltage-gated calcium channels.
source: As such, mechano-signal triggered ASIC1a, essentially a sodium channel, results in the intracellular calcium elevation possibly by activating voltage-gated calcium channels (Boillat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on inference and citation to related work.

claim: ASIC1a is N-glycosylated at N366 and N393, both residues extracellularly located.
source: ASIC1a is N-glycosylated at N366 and N393, both residues extracellular located (Jing et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: N-glycosylation is reported to be involved in the surface trafficking and dendritic spine trafficking of ASIC1.
source: While N-glycosylation is reported to be involved in the surface trafficking and dendritic spine trafficking of ASIC1 (Jing et al., 2012; Kadurin et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: N-glycosylation of many proteins has been known to be important for adhesion and migration.
source: the N-glycosylation of many proteins has been known to be important for adhesion and migration (Gu, 2012; Medina-Cano et al., 2018; Stevens and Spang, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: When ultrasound is applied to the brain, the acoustic pressure exerted through extracellular matrices can possibly activate ASIC1a via a cytoskeletal-dependent manner.
source: When ultrasound is applied to the brain, the acoustic pressure exerted through extracellular matrixes, can possibly activate ASIC1a via a cytoskeletal-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: DCX has been accepted as a surrogate mark for neurogenesis in dentate gyrus.
source: Since DCX has been accepted as a surrogate mark for neurogenesis in dentate gyrus (Jin et al., 2010; Salvi et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased DCX-positive cells in dentate gyrus with a consecutive 3 day of ultrasound treatment suggests a therapeutic implication.
source: increased DCX-positive cells in dentate gyrus with a consecutive 3 day of ultrasound treatment suggests a therapeutic implication.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DCX staining results.

claim: DCX plays multiple roles in brain development including hippocampal pyramidal neuronal lamination, cortical neuronal migration, and axonal wiring.
source: Of note, DCX plays multiple roles in brain development including hippocampal pyramidal neuronal lamination, cortical neuronal migration, and axonal wiring (Germain et al., 2013; Koizumi et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The use of ultrasound in developing brains should be extremely cautious.
source: The use of ultrasound in developing brains should be extremely cautious.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on knowledge about DCX's role in brain development.

claim: A clinically safe low-intensity transcranial ultrasound could modulate neuronal activity in mouse brain.
source: In conclusion, here we provide evidence that a clinically safely low-intensity transcranial ultrasound could modulate neuronal activity in mouse brain.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Low-intensity ultrasound can directly activate neurons via ASIC1a, which provides a molecular basis for future development of ultrasound neuromodulation.
source: The low-intensity ultrasound can directly activate neurons via ASIC1a, which provides a molecular basis for future development of ultrasound neuromodulation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results and their implications.

claim: High-intensity transcranial ultrasound can elicit a startle-like motor response via an indirect auditory mechanism.
source: A study showed high-intensity transcranial ultrasound can elicit a startle-like motor response via an indirect auditory mechanism (Sato et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ultrasound at pressure level above 0.5 MPa can activate neurons in living organisms via engineered TRP-4 channels in worm model.
source: Emerging sonogenetics in worm model also identified and engineered TRP-4 channels as a sensor for the ultrasound stimulus to activate neurons in living organisms at pressure level above 0.5 MPa (Ibsen et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ultrasound at 0.1 MPa acoustic pressure was found to activate neurons via Piezo one mechanosensitive ion channel.
source: and ultrasound at 0.1 MPa acoustic pressure was found to activate neurons via Piezo one mechanosensitive ion channel (Qiu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The energy intensity or acoustic pressure of most clinical trials or basic researches used for BBB opening or neuromodulation are both high, and safety issue of this technique in clinical application remains a concern.
source: Nonetheless, the energy intensity or acoustic pressure of most clinical trials or basic researches used for BBB opening or neuromodulation are both high, and safety issue of this technique in clinical application remains a concern.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of the field and cited literature.

claim: A much lower intensity ultrasound at the order lower than 10 mW/cm² is proposed to activate neurons via mechanosensitive ion channels in mammals' brain for potential clinical application.
source: In this study, a much lower intensity ultrasound at the order lower than 10 mW/cm2 is proposed to activate neurons via mechanosensitive ion channels in mammals' brain for potential clinical application.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's objective and approach.

claim: Mechanosensitive ion channels such as PIEZO and TRP channels and acid sensing ion channels (ASICs) are considered the candidates likely responsive to ultrasound.
source: Mechanosensitve ion channels such as PIEZO and TRP channels and acid sensing ion channels (ASICs) (Cheng et al., 2018; Murthy et al., 2017; Nilius and Honoré, 2012) are considered the candidates likely responsive to ultrasound.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on knowledge of mechanosensitive channels and citations to relevant literature.

claim: The phosphorylation of extracellular-signal-regulated kinase (p-ERK) is an established indicator of immediate neuronal activation.
source: The phosphorylation of extracellular-signal-regulated kinase (p-ERK), an established indicator of immediate neuronal activation (Gao and Ji, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The intensity used for in vivo animal experiments was 5 mW/cm² (ISPTA), and 7.4 mW/cm² (ISPPA, at 700 mVpp) for micropipette in vitro experiment.
source: The intensity used for in vivo animal experiments was 5 mW/cm2 (ISPTA), and 7.4 mW/cm2 (ISPPA, at 700 mVpp) for micropipette in vitro experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental parameters used.

claim: These intensity values are within the range of not causing any side effects from ultrasound, like heat and cavitation.
source: These intensity values are within the range of not causing any side effects from ultrasound, like heat and cavitation.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of ultrasound safety parameters.

claim: Asic1−/− mice were generated by crossing Asic1 conditional KO (Asic1f/f) mice with protamine-Cre mice.
source: Asic1−/− mice were a gift from Dr. CC Lien of NYCU of Taiwan and generated by crossing Asic1 conditional KO (Asic1f/f) mice (Wu, 2013) with protamine-Cre mice (Lin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how the knockout mice were generated, supported by citations.

claim: Asic3-knockout/eGFP-f-knockin mice (Asic3-/-) were generated based on the Accn3 gene with a targeting allele containing a 6 kb long arm and a 240 bp short arm for homologous recombination.
source: Asic3-knockout/eGFP-f-knockin mice (Asic3-/-) were generated based on the Accn3 gene; in brief the design was mainly the targeting allele with a 6 kb long arm (HincII∼HincII DNA fragment located 82 bp downstream the transcription start site) and a 240 bp short arm upstream of the ATG translation start site of Accn3 was used for homologous recombination (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about how the knockout mice were generated, supported by citation.
